en.title: White House website debuts 5 retro arcade video games that promote Trump’s agenda
en.description: A White House website featuring arcade games is photographed on a computer screen Thursday, Sept. 3, 2026. (AP Photo/Jon Elswick)
en.fullContent:
A White House website featuring arcade games is photographed on a computer screen Thursday, Sept. 3, 2026. (AP Photo/Jon Elswick)

President Donald Trump speaks during an event to present the Congressional Space Medal of Honor to Artemis II crew members, Friday, Aug. 28, 2026, at Johnson Space Center in Houston. (AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein)

WASHINGTON (AP) — The White House website on Thursday unveiled Arcade, a collection of five low-resolution video games that promote different aspects of President Donald Trump’s agenda.

“Build the Wall” is a “Tetris” knockoff that transforms the classic game into an effort to “Protect the border from the coming horde.” In “Rio Run,” which resembles the mobile favorite “Snake,” an icon resembling Trump runs around gathering potential border crossers.

In “Supply Line,” which looks like a condensed version of the arcade game “Tapper,” food moves along an assembly line and you must reject items that don’t meet “Make America Healthy Again” standards.

Two of the games take place over the skies of the nation’s capital. In “Flappy Bill,” an eagle carries a bill across the National Mall. In “Trump Savings Tycoon,” your goal is to collect money flying through the air to “Fill your kids’ Trump Accounts,” the administration savings plan that offers $1,000 to every child born during Trump’s term.

en.title: He Was Supposed To Play Video Games With His Friend — But Radio Silence Made Him Drive Over To Check On Him
en.description: The guy who wrote this story found out in a hurry that his best friend wasn’t too happy after he checked in on him because he was worried about his...
en.fullContent:
The guy who wrote this story found out in a hurry that his best friend wasn’t too happy after he checked in on him because he was worried about his well-being.

Get all the details below, and see if you think he might’ve taken things too far.

“I (30M) and my best friend Darren (29M) sometimes we play video games together since I’ve met him.

He is my ex boyfriend and I know there’s always that thing of “don’t stay friends with your ex” but it’s been over 3 years since he broke up with me and usually we’re petty civil and jokey about most things when we hang out or play video games which has mainly been Fortnite since Day 1.

We started dating back in June 2022 then when he broke up with me in May 2023 it was with respect and agreed to stay friends.

So the point of this post is to see if I was in the wrong to the following: Last night we were ready to make a PlayStation party because I asked him around 10 pm if he was ready and he said yes. So I did and then I got on Fortnite.

en.title: There Is No Greater Joy In Video Games Than Laying Down Some Overwatch And Watching An Absolute Fool Walk Straight Into It
en.description: I have been playing a lot of Star Wars Zero Company this week, and for all the things it does very well--most of which we'll probably get to over t...
en.fullContent:
I have been playing a lot of Star Wars Zero Company this week, and for all the things it does very well--most of which we'll probably get to over the next week or two--there's only one thing that is so good it made me literally hoot out loud at my computer screen.

That thing, as XCOM lovers will have worked out already from the headline, is Overwatch. If you've never played those games (or any of the many other tactics games that use a similar system with a similar name), Overwatch is where you sacrifice a small amount of your current turn's action points in order to direct a unit to cover a certain part of the map with their gun, and if an enemy unit enters that part of the map (usually depicted as a cone of vision) during their turn then your unit will shoot at it.

"But why not just shoot at it in your turn?" someone who hasn't played any of these games might be asking, to which I'll say, "Great question! Here's why". You see, in turn-based tactics games, cover is usually a big deal. If you shoot at an enemy unit while they're hunkered down behind some crates, or around a corner and out of sight, you're wasting your turn (and some bullets) on a target you're very unlikely to hit.

If you wait until you can catch them moving during their turn, though, you've got them dead to rights. An enemy unit running across an Overwatch cone has their weapon down, their gaze focused elsewhere and are usually completely out of cover. They're like First World War soldiers trying to cross No Man's Land, they're like lambs being led to slaughter, they're like rubes getting shot to hell because they walked directly into my trap.

Overwatch rules because while nothing has materially changed in terms of outcome of a battle if you use it--you've shot at and killed some enemies, same as you would have otherwise--the way it's packaged makes you feel like the smartest guy in the room. Like someone who would say in a very whiny voice "You fool, you idiots, you had perfectly good cover! Now you've met your end because of my devious plan!"

Zero Company also very smartly continues the XCOM tradition of telling the player that when enemy reinforcements are on the way, they will be coming from this exact spot on the map, and so if you as the player decide to setup multiple overlapping Overwatch fields across that spawnpoint, and a group of enemies show up and the first thing they do is walk into a hail of blaster fire that makes you jump up and down in your seat clapping, then that's just a thing that's going to happen in this video game. A lot.

en.title: Researchers Reveal the Hidden High Cost of “Free-To-Play” Video Games
en.description: A game may be free to download, but for a small group of players, the spending can become anything but small.
en.fullContent:
A game may be free to download, but for a small group of players, the spending can become anything but small.

Video games are a major source of entertainment for teenagers and adults, and many of the most popular titles now use a “free-to-play” business model. Players can begin without paying (‘free-to-play’ games), but they are repeatedly offered virtual items, upgrades, subscriptions, and other purchases known as microtransactions. Although these transactions are optional, modern games can be carefully designed to make spending feel natural, urgent, and difficult to resist.

The word “microtransaction” also understates how much money may be involved. A single purchase can cost €100 (about $117) or more, which is hardly a minor expense, especially for a child or teenager. Many players spend only small amounts, but averages can hide the behavior of the comparatively few users who provide much of the revenue.

Loot boxes have attracted particular scrutiny because they allow players to buy randomized rewards (the contents of which are unknown at the time of purchase). The combination of payment, uncertainty, and the possibility of receiving a desirable item has led researchers and regulators to compare them with gambling.

Yet chance-based rewards are only one part of the free-to-play economy. Battle passes, rotating stores, virtual currencies, paid progression, personalized offers, and time-limited events can all encourage repeated purchases. Some create urgency by making items available briefly, while others add extra steps between real money and the final price. A bundle of gems or tokens can make it harder to recognize how much an item actually costs.

Our research found that microtransaction spending was heavily concentrated. The highest-spending 10%, whom we called “heavy spenders” rather than the gambling industry term “whales,” accounted for most of the money spent. The gap between this small group and everyone else was strikingly similar to the spending inequality found in gambling.

en.title: The Research-Backed Reasons I'm Fine With My Kid Playing Video Games
en.description: When I was in elementary school, back in the 8-bit Nintendo days, every once in a while my father, older sister, and I would get together and try t...
en.fullContent:
When I was in elementary school, back in the 8-bit Nintendo days, every once in a while my father, older sister, and I would get together and try to play our favorite video game—Super Mario Bros. 3—straight through without warping. We would attempt the feat as one, unified Mario, each passing the controller to the next person whenever someone died or completed a level. We had to strategize together about our best paths through the obstacles and the optimal usage of items, and when it was time for lunch or dinner we would pause the game but leave the TV on, because it wasn’t possible to save our progress. These are perhaps some of my favorite childhood memories.

So when my daughter was younger and begging for a game console of her own, as a Super Mario fan, I really had no objections. I envisioned us on the couch together playing through all the levels of Kirby and the Forgotten Land, employing the same level of teamwork my family used on our Super Mario Saturdays. (I’m grateful, though, that we wouldn’t have to do it all in one shot anymore—thank you, SD cards, for the ability to save games!)

As a parent, though, I’m told I have to be wary of letting my daughter have too much screen time. Video games, other parents warn on social media and in group chats, will make her sedentary and smooth-brained, and keep her shut off in her room isolated, lonely, and depressed.

But is any of that actually true? None of it seems to line up with my own experiences gaming. In fact, last time I got a visit from my father, who’s now in his 70s, he still played Nintendo with us—three generations on one couch, each trying to best the others in Mario Party. And games have only gotten better, with more involved storytelling, deeper character development, and more sophisticated puzzles, since my side-scrolling adventures. How can playing them be across-the-board bad?

I set out to look into what research really says about kids, games, and gaming, and I learned it’s not really helpful for caregivers to paint every activity that takes place on an electronic device with the same scary “screen time” brush. And while there are definite traps to watch out for when letting kids play video games—in-game purchases, for example, along with unrestricted communication with other players, and a temptation to play instead of sleep—researchers showed me that there’s actually a great many benefits to kids playing video games they might not get from other, more passive on-screen activities like scrolling, posting, or watching shows or videos. (More than one researcher even compared video games favorably to reading books—which is equally stationary and up-close, but a lot less interactive—but the parent group chat isn’t ready for that yet.) And, based on their data, here’s why I’ve gone from believing that not only is it okay to let kids play video games, but adults should actually encourage kids to play.

It’s an accusation I’ve heard even in my 8-bit days: Video games will rot your brain. And while the aphorism persists to this day, it’s actually the opposite that’s true. Kids who play video games actually outperform non-gamers on cognitive tests, research shows. But the idea that video games are bad for kids’ brains is so entrenched that, even when I told friends what I learned while I was working on this article, they didn’t believe me. (“Hmm yeah I’m going to go with no on that,” my college roommate, now a guidance counselor, texted me when I told her what I’d found out. But maybe it’s because I could beat her at every game except Dr. Mario.)
